name: ADÉLA
resolved: Adéla Jergová, b. 27 Nov 2003, Bratislava, Slovakia; trained in ballet; cut early from The Debut: Dream Academy (2023); signed to Capitol (Polydor UK). Debut album PRIMA released 2026-09-04, 11 tracks, executive producers Dylan Brady and Blake Slatkin. Singles: KGB (2026-04-16), Red Bottoms (2026-06-11), Ain't In LA (2026-07-22), Nicole Kidman. Earlier: Homewrecked (independent), SexOnTheBeat. UK: Nicole Kidman No. 4 and Ain't In LA No. 12 (chart dated 2026-09-25); album UK No. 2; US Billboard 200 debut No. 4 (chart week unverified).

characteristics.text: Says she is blunt by culture and dry and sarcastic; uses humour to carry things that aren't funny.

Titles are often loaded proper nouns or brands (KGB, Nicole Kidman, Red Bottoms, Hitachi, Marijuana); in every case she explains, the noun stands for a feeling (a corset moment = feeling like a movie star; a worn shoe = feeling run down), not the topic.

Place or identity as stance: Ain't In LA defines the narrator by refusing the famous city, moving from one specific girl (verse 1, domestic detail) to girls everywhere (verse 2), with a pitched-down male refrain by Theron Thomas.
Mixes registers on purpose: swagger with vulnerability, witty with deep; pushed herself into love songs for this album after avoiding them.
Comic literal personas (KGB as a spy absorbing American culture) can be misread as metaphor or politics; she added a disclaimer in the video.
Spoken friend-banter between sections (Boys, with Lara Raj) for comedy and attitude.

Critics split: Rolling Stone wants her deadpan and showing not telling; NME wants her winking; both punished lines that stated the obvious. Sincere/slow tracks (Therapy, Hitachi, Marijuana) drew the most criticism.

Ain't In LA, examined whole: a pronoun ladder, third-person portrait (she) in verse 1, 'you' in the second pre-chorus and verse 2, the first 'I' only in the chorus; a tribute to her mother turned into an address to other girls.
characteristics.evidence: SP-F8 observable_feature via tool paraphrase; SP-S8 documented_statement

characteristics.text: The title names only the place it rejects; LA is the lyric's only named place and the affirmed place is never named, which listeners filled with their hometowns and critics wanted filled with Bratislava.
Refuses LA's monopoly from inside (she lives there and likes it) rather than attacking the city.
A second voice (Theron Thomas, pitched down per press) carries a status-image refrain with no 'I' and stands in for a bridge.
characteristics.evidence: SP-F11 observable_feature, low confidence on its meaning

variation: Her upbeat singles and her ballads are received very differently; Therapy was cut from a 15-minute ramble and judged simple, while Hitachi was called terrific by Clash and a slog by a user reviewer. Treat 'ADÉLA' as a reference for attitude, camp, blunt humour and proper-noun hooks, not for ballad writing.
uncertain: Per-track writer credits rest on an uncited Wikipedia table except Ain't In LA, Hitachi, Nicole Kidman and (producer only) I'm The Man. No statement from her about writing in English as a second language; nothing from Brady or Slatkin about the sessions; no documented changed lines.

coverage: Per-track writer credits for all 11 PRIMA tracks now read from Qobuz distributor credits (SP-S3), replacing the uncited Wikipedia table; they match it, including Therapy's unusual producer list. One unverified anomaly: the extract shows no Jergová writing credit on KGB. notes: 4 characteristics added from the song-analysis round; coverage rewritten

name: Sabrina Carpenter room (Carpenter / Allen / Antonoff / Bunetta / Jones)
resolved: Sabrina Carpenter (US pop). Short n' Sweet (2024): Espresso (2024-04-11; Carpenter, Allen, Julian Bunetta, Steph Jones), Please Please Please (2024-06-06; Carpenter, Allen, Jack Antonoff), Taste. Man's Best Friend (2025): Manchild (Carpenter, Allen, Antonoff), Tears. Credits verified per track in AA-S* and PA-S* records.

characteristics.text: Lyrics are often literal things Carpenter said in conversation; she sings as acting, picturing the person, moving between sung and spoken phrasing; likes a line sung sweetly that turns blunt two seconds later.
Humour before hurt: sincere line, then the joke that undercuts it (Please Please Please bridge); subjects picked because they can be framed as funny.
Hooks can arrive from sung improvisation over a groove with no concept (Espresso: 20-minute burst, then hours of word changes); a 'silly' line kept because it sat on the melody.
Spoken interjection at the top (Manchild's eye roll) sets fond exasperation, partly at herself, before any insult.
Limit: by Man's Best Friend, critics (Slant, Guardian, Independent, LA Times) found the puns, innuendo and profanity overused and 'reaching for a memeable lyric'.

Please Please Please, examined whole: the chorus runs from politest to bluntest (tripled polite title, a petty makeup stake, a line ranking heartbreak below ego, the profane word last); Carpenter says that passage was the most deliberately shaped and its last word an ad lib with the melody pushed lower.
characteristics.evidence: SP-F2 documented_statement; SP-F3 observable_feature via tool paraphrase

characteristics.text: A fantasy verse is set apart harmonically (Antonoff: A to C on verse 2) and the return pops the bubble; the fantasy is retracted as a joke with some truth in it.
The narrator is built to be pitied and feared at once (Antonoff's Dolly model: sad but not to be messed with).

variation: Espresso (nonsense-adjacent confidence) and Please Please Please (polite plea with an edge) and Manchild (insults on a sweet tune) use different mechanisms; do not reduce the room to 'cheeky'.
uncertain: No writer statements on Taste or Tears; Manchild's writing process undocumented beyond its opening gesture.
note: Reference summary for translating a named reference into editable qualities. Never an instruction to imitate or reproduce.
coverage: Now rests on one whole-song examination (Please Please Please, via the Song Exploder transcript and a press print of the lyric, both seen only through tool extraction) plus process accounts for Espresso and Manchild. Does not cover Taste, Tears or any Man's Best Friend lyric as a whole work; no official lyric presentation was accessed.

notes: 3 characteristics added from the song-analysis round; coverage rewritten

name: Nashville writers' room (Morgan Wallen catalogue)
resolved: Morgan Wallen (US country) as performer; writers include Ashley Gorley, John Byron, Jacob Kasher Hindlin, Charlie Handsome (Ryan Vojtesak), ERNEST, Chandler Walters, Post Malone. Last Night (2023), I Had Some Help (2024, with Post Malone), Love Somebody (2024; 6 writers per label, 11 per Wikipedia), I'm the Problem (2025 album, 37 tracks). Comparison hits: Shaboozey A Bar Song (Tipsy) (2024), Ella Langley & Riley Green you look like you love me (2024), Zach Bryan (sole writer).
sample: you look like you love me
requested_by: Sam, 9 Oct 2026 (Morgan Wallen as one of three differing directions); comparison group, not a template

characteristics.text: Beat/loop first, hook tested first, fast writes to a fixed artist target (Last Night from an 8-bar voice-note loop; I Had Some Help in about 24 minutes); Handsome concedes a hit hook can carry weak verses.

Titles from room talk with tense/person shifted into an admission; idiom flips (When It Rains It Pours); the detail that makes a title true for the singer (Sangria); sing-testing a title (Runnin' Outta Moonlight 'sang better').
Everyday phrases with a second reading that moves the blame or means 'the end' (Last Night, I'm the Problem, Lies Lies Lies); fights left unresolved.
Spoken 'talking country' verses under a sung chorus (you look like you love me).

Limits admitted from inside: McAnally calls the trend 'a rearranging of the same thing' and writes it too; Gorley says big co-writing teams and radio pressure produce songs that don't come from the soul; critics find I'm the Problem formulaic (whiskey, drives, exes); Chartmetric links more writers per song to more repeated words (correlation only).

The Love Junkies (McKenna, Lindsey, Rose) on 'Girl Crush': the title came first with no agreed meaning. Lindsey's sung opening, played by ear in 6/8, chose the angle. The writers' only check was whether the jealousy made sense (they never imagined the same-sex reading). The phone memo was kept instead of making a demo, and McKenna praises the band's restraint on the record.
'Girl Crush' states its misleadable title in line one and settles it with a plain reason in the chorus (an explanation payoff). Five-stanza form, no bridge.
characteristics.evidence: observable_feature (tool-described lyric block SC-S5, licence unverified; SC-S6)

characteristics.text: Zach Bryan is the sole-writer outlier. 'Something in the Orange' (2022-04-22) is an image title that began, on his first account, from the word 'orange'. The title is a frame whose verdict changes from hope to loss. No pre-chorus or bridge. Vocal and guitar were tracked live with light overdubs, in a day. It reached Hot 100 No. 10 without country radio. His origin stories conflict: a cabin sunset, or being stood up on a date.
characteristics.evidence: documented_statement, relayed (SC-S16, SC-S17, CW-S49; producer CW-S48); observable_feature (SC-S14, SC-S15)

variation: The craft moves (flip, revealing detail, sing-test, cull the B song) are separable from the imagery (drink, truck, small town) and the blame-trading persona. Zach Bryan is the sole-writer outlier.
uncertain: No first-hand craft interview with John Byron or Jacob Kasher Hindlin; no transcript of Gorley's Songcraft episode on Last Night; release dates missing for the I'm the Problem single, Something in the Orange and Lies Lies Lies; several sources predate 2023.
note: Reference summary for translating a named reference into editable qualities. Never an instruction to imitate or reproduce.
coverage: These additions rest on two songs: 'Girl Crush' (2014, a Nashville trio writing for a band) and 'Something in the Orange' (2022, a sole writer outside the radio system). Neither is from the Morgan Wallen catalogue the profile is built on; they widen its comparison group and do not describe Wallen's room. They fill the profile's missing release date for 'Something in the Orange': 2022-04-22 (SC-S16, SC-S19).

notes: 3 characteristics added from the song-analysis round; coverage rewritten

name: Noah Kahan (Stick Season)
resolved: Noah Kahan (US folk-pop). Stick Season (2022; built in public: verse posted, chorus written 29 Oct, second verse after fans asked). Song Exploder transcript used.
sample: The View Between Villages (writer statement only)

characteristics.text: Chorus sung in a borrowed country twang to get outside himself; kept the verse's chords because a folk song should stay simple.

Feared Vermont specificity would alienate outsiders; the particular is what connected; a late line came from literally living in Strafford after friends left; second verse on family depression took days and was kept because the discomfort might help someone.
Last-chorus lift from harmony and gang vocals rather than new words; staging the lyric literally was judged a bit corny.

Carries a whole relationship on one plain physical metaphor: in Stick Season the other person passes his exit and keeps driving. He says he chose driving to show someone who wants to leave, or be left, but can't.

Puts his own share of the blame on the record and makes the self-pity forgivable by naming it; he describes the song as knowing some of it is your fault. The morning sketch's clinical self-label became a confessed behaviour ('play the victim') in the posted chorus.
characteristics.evidence: documented_statement (ST-S1) + observable_feature (SS-F12, sketch vs posted chorus, tool-extracted)

characteristics.text: Uses a regional seasonal term as the relationship's in-between state, chosen because it is regional. He means the bleak picture to be hopeful (the season ends) and calls the last line acceptance of what is left.

Beyond Stick Season: holds his ambivalence about home in a single turn of phrase (Homesick: wishing he were home against being tired of being there), and shapes an arrangement to follow a lyric's emotional route (The View Between Villages: calm, then frantic nearing his old house, then settled, with a long organ close).

Has a separate co-writing mode: Hurt Somebody was written with Scott Harris in Nashville in about 25 minutes after an unproductive session, aiming to tell the other side of a break-up cleverly, and he says about half of his second album was co-written. The interviewer, not Kahan, says he wrote 10 of the 14 songs on the Stick Season album alone. Gabe Simon is a credited co-writer on Northern Attitude (ST-S5).
characteristics.evidence: documented_statement (SS-S8 Q4-Q5) + interviewer claim (SS-S8 intro) + credits (ST-S5)

characteristics.text: Correction to the existing gang-vocal note: it was his management who said the big gang vocal might be corny for so intimate a song. He agreed, spent a long time re-recording with more weight on harmonies, and says a more nuanced way was possible.
Production aim on Stick Season: keep the casual, not self-serious energy of the phone demo; the first take was guitar and vocal to a click.

Accounts of where Stick Season began differ slightly: in his LA Airbnb around the sessions for his second album (ST-S1), or late at night on the way back from one of those sessions, as a folkier escape from a pop track (SS-S8 Q8). Treat the origin as approximate.

variation: Single-song depth; the 'folk simplicity' rule is his for this song.
uncertain: Who called the gang vocal corny is unclear in the transcript; whether the regional term did the work is untested.
note: Reference summary for translating a named reference into editable qualities. Never an instruction to imitate or reproduce.
coverage: One song examined as a whole work: Stick Season (2022-07-08), with partial lyric access through the Song Exploder 247 excerpts. Writer statements, without any lyric examined, on Northern Attitude (subject only), Homesick, The View Between Villages and Hurt Somebody. Sources: ST-S1, ST-S3, ST-S4, ST-S5, SS-S8, SS-S9. Not covered: anything after the 2022 album and its deluxe editions, including the album announced for April 2026 (SS-S12, not examined); Busyhead-era lyrics beyond one remark; any co-written song examined as a whole; what Gabe Simon contributes as a writer; Kahan's humour beyond Stick Season. Nothing was checked against recordings. This is a one-song-deep profile with thin catalogue notes; do not treat Stick Season as the whole of him.

notes: 8 characteristics added from the song-analysis round; coverage rewritten

name: Sam Fender
resolved: Sam Fender, English singer-songwriter and guitarist from North Shields, Tyne and Wear; he says he had lived there all his life as of 2021 (SS-S6). Sole credited writer on both songs checked and on every standard-edition track of People Watching (SS-S4, SS-S7). Works with a long-standing band (Joe Atkinson, Dean Thompson, Dru Michael) and, on People Watching, with producer Adam Granduciel of The War on Drugs. Press files him under heartland rock (SS-S3, SS-S11).
sample: People Watching (single 2024-11-15; title track of People Watching, 2025-02-21): examined as a whole work, partial lyric
Seventeen Going Under (single 2021-07-07; title track of his second album): writer statements on subject and origin only, lyric not examined

characteristics.text: Prefers plain description to metaphor. He singles out Springsteen's best lyrics as plain description with no metaphor that makes a scene immediately vivid, admires Kendrick Lamar's sense of place and the ballads of Suzanne Vega and Tracy Chapman, and contrasts this with pop's simple love-or-sex stories.

Starts from a personal loss or hardship and widens it to his town and the country. People Watching walks from a deathbed into the cost-of-living crisis, homelessness and guilt at his own success; Seventeen Going Under ties his mother's illness and the DWP's treatment of her to the state of the country.

Sets sad or yearning words to uplifting, driving music on purpose. He chose a euphoric, liberating feel for People Watching to reach the acceptance stage of grief, says he prefers yearning and hopeful to happy, and admires ABBA's sad lyrics on uplifting music. He says his label sometimes asks him for happier songs.
Writes as an adult looking back at a younger self: he began Seventeen Going Under during about two years of therapy, about things he could not have put into words at 17.

Revised a chorus by changing its subject rather than its wording: the People Watching chorus that summed up his town and his own tragedy was replaced months later by one made of observed strangers and a borrowed grave inscription ('Somebody's Sweetheart').

Process: a song starts from a melody or chord progression or from a lyric; the melody-first ones tend to become singles. Demos are phone loops (drums, piano, bass) over which he finds lyric and melody. He says he doesn't know where a song is going until he gets there and that a good song can't be forced. Most songs come quickly; People Watching, months in the making, was the exception.
In People Watching the person the song is for is addressed only late (the vigil line, the middle eight, the final promise); the rest is first-person observation.

Writes alone. Band and producers shape the arrangement and production (Granduciel's straight beat and synth, the binaural acoustic take, strings arranged by Rosie Danvers), not the credited writing. The one co-write found is the deluxe-edition Rein Me In, with Olivia Dean and Max Wolfgang.
A stubborn chorus: the first one wasn't good enough for the subject, so the song waited months.

uncertain: Rests on one song examined as a whole work; see coverage.
coverage: Rests on one song examined as a whole work (People Watching, with partial lyric via the Song Exploder 298 excerpts; its second verse known only from press) and on writer statements about one other (Seventeen Going Under: subject and origin, nothing at lyric level). Sources: SS-S1, SS-S2, SS-S3, SS-S4, SS-S5, SS-S6, SS-S7, SS-S10, SS-S11. Not covered: his debut album and earlier singles; every other song on the two albums; the deluxe-edition and later songs; any lyric-level account of Seventeen Going Under; songs in other registers (he describes the People Watching album as stories of everyday characters, and none of those were examined); any revision except the People Watching chorus. Nothing was checked against recordings. Two songs, both about loss and his town, are not the catalogue: do not reduce him to grief anthems or protest songs.

name: Lewis Capaldi

characteristics.text: Melody first: brings a parked verse and pre-chorus melody to the room, and the lyric is finished fast and collaboratively there. Accounts of the details conflict.
Deliberately widened scope: from one breakup to loss in general, so the song fits a breakup and bereavements. His own later accounts of the subject vary.
Plain, image-light, wholly sincere lyric carried by melody and a raw vocal; critics call it generic by design.
The humour stays outside the songs, in the public persona; he says humour is what lets him own his flaws.
Sparse arrangement with TMS: piano and voice, drums rejected, strings only in the middle eight.

name: Adele

characteristics.text: Arrives with the story and the opening verse lines; the co-writer's role is music, simplicity and protecting the plain words.
Deliberately personal frame: a real situation (a married ex, an uninvited visit), not generalised.
The irony is carried by one qualifier in the title and chorus, which are sung straight.
Demo as record: the first sincere take, piano and voice, kept over an orchestral version.

name: Sam Smith

characteristics.text: Honest, direct phrasing over clever wording, on chords with enough space to speak over.
Refused a bridge the label asked for, because the song had said what it needed and the space was for the crowd.
A choir built from layered takes of one voice in different registers; strings only near the end.
Changed a gendered word years later so the song could still be sung truthfully.
